title: Beyond Language
author: The Mindful Manager
summary: The Mindful Manager argues that how and when feedback is delivered matters as much as the words chosen. The piece opens with a story of a senior director who gave three enthusiastic colleagues about twenty points of well-phrased feedback in a single thirty-minute meeting after a year of silence, leaving them fighting back tears. Citing Kluger and DeNisi's meta-analysis of 23,663 observations, the author notes that over a third of feedback interventions reduced performance, especially when they shifted attention from the task to the self. The remedy is a better feedback system: give feedback in the moment so it attaches to one behaviour, favour regular informal conversations over annual appraisals, and make feedback a flow in all directions through 360 reviews, team discussions and open floors. An annual review should only summarise what people have already heard. The closing line is that you are not your feedback, you are a work in progress.
points: Impeccable language cannot rescue feedback that arrives as a year of accumulated criticism delivered in half an hour.
Research shows feedback backfires when it directs attention to the self instead of the task, so it must be specific enough to change the work without diminishing the person.
Timely feedback attaches to a single event and reads as something to learn from rather than a verdict on identity.
Informal, regular conversations remove the appraisal weight that makes people defensive and keep the focus on learning.
Annual reviews should summarise earlier discussions, and feedback should flow upward and sideways through 360 reviews, team discussions and open forums.
quotes: And it made me think: even when the language is impeccable, the feedback is constructive and the intention is positive, the way we deliver feedback can still have a very different impact from the one we intended.
Their Feedback Intervention Theory suggests feedback becomes less effective when it shifts our attention away from the task and towards ourselves.
Feedback should be specific enough to change the work without being personal enough to diminish the person.
But there’s another part of the feedback equation that deserves just as much attention: the system around it, how and when we deliver it.

Your team is much more likely to connect your feedback to a specific behaviour rather than their identity because your message relates to one event or one behaviour that could have been approached differently.
Your annual review should be an opportunity to summarise the discussions you’ve had throughout the year. It shouldn’t be the first time someone hears developmental feedback.
When feedback becomes part of our everyday working lives, in formal and informal settings, it becomes easier to receive because it carries less weight.
Leaders need to create environments where feedback flows regularly and in all directions, so that it becomes a normal part of how we work rather than something that carries the weight of a judgement.
